paragraphs: Machine unlearning aims to remove information associated with particular training samples from an already trained model. Evaluating whether removal worked is difficult. A common approach uses membership inference attacks, which try to determine whether a sample belonged to the training data. This paper examines reliability problems in the metrics used for that evaluation.

The authors formulate evaluation as a cryptographic game between an unlearning algorithm and an adversary performing membership inference. The rules of this game induce a metric for measuring removal efficacy. This connects the evaluation score to a formal adversarial setting and gives it provable guarantees that existing metrics do not satisfy.

The paper also develops an efficient practical approximation to the induced metric, supported by theoretical analysis and empirical experiments. Its contribution concerns how to assess unlearning algorithms: it provides a more principled connection between an attack-based test and the removal behavior that test is intended to measure. That connection can support more reliable comparisons when developing unlearning methods.
neurips-2025-a-reliable-cryptographic-fr.tldr: A cryptographic game provides a principled metric and practical approximation for evaluating machine unlearning through membership inference attacks.

paragraphs: Care-PD addresses the shortage of diverse, clinically annotated movement data for assessing walking in Parkinson’s disease. It brings together nine cohorts from eight clinical centers. Recordings originating from ordinary video or motion capture pass through a shared preprocessing pipeline that converts them into anonymized SMPL body meshes, giving the collection a common representation.

The dataset supports both clinical prediction and learning from movement structure. Its benchmarks include predicting UPDRS gait scores, lifting two-dimensional keypoints into three dimensions, and reconstructing the full body in three dimensions. Clinical prediction is evaluated through four protocols covering performance within datasets, transfer across datasets, exclusion of one dataset during training, and adaptation using multiple datasets.

In the reported comparisons, learned motion encoders consistently outperform handcrafted gait features. Pretraining on Care-PD reduces mean joint-position error from 60.8 to 7.5 millimeters and improves severity macro-F1 by 17%. These findings support the value of diverse clinical motion data for both reconstruction and severity assessment. The dataset and benchmark code are released for non-commercial research.
neurips-2025-care-pd-a-multi-site-anonym.tldr: Care-PD combines anonymized gait data from eight clinical centers to improve movement representation learning and Parkinson’s severity assessment.

paragraphs: CHOICE evaluates how well vision-language models understand remote sensing imagery. Although both general-purpose and specialized models have shown promise in Earth observation, the paper identifies a need for systematic evaluation across the different capabilities this domain requires. Its contribution is a benchmark organized around those capabilities.

The benchmark separates perception from reasoning, then divides them into six secondary dimensions and 23 individual tasks. It contains 10,507 multiple-choice problems built from data spanning 50 cities around the world. Data collection, question construction, and quality control are designed to support reliable questions with definitive answers. This format makes scoring straightforward while the hierarchy gives the assessment broader coverage than a single task.

The authors evaluate three proprietary models and 21 open-source models. Their results reveal critical limitations in remote sensing despite the models’ broader capabilities. CHOICE therefore supplies a structured way to examine what these systems can do in a specialized visual domain and where their performance remains inadequate. The stated findings establish the need for this evaluation without identifying a particular model as universally best.
neurips-2025-choice-benchmarking-the-rem.tldr: CHOICE tests remote sensing perception and reasoning with 10,507 questions, revealing limitations across 24 vision-language models.

paragraphs: Deep hedging uses learned strategies to manage financial exposure. This paper examines what happens when the distribution of inputs differs from the one a strategy was trained on. The authors first show that standard deep hedging models can suffer substantial performance degradation under small distributional perturbations, making distribution mismatch a central robustness concern.

Their response is an adversarial training framework that challenges a strategy with changes to an entire distribution. The adversarial optimization searches within a Wasserstein ball, which specifies a neighborhood of distributions. The paper provides a computationally tractable reformulation of this problem so that training against these distributional changes becomes practical.

Across the numerical experiments, adversarially trained strategies consistently perform better than classical counterparts outside the training sample and under model misspecification. Additional results show reliable performance on real market data and during periods of market change. These findings support the framework as a way to improve robustness in the tested settings, connecting the distributional training objective to performance under the kinds of uncertainty examined in the study.
neurips-2025-distributional-adversarial-.tldr: Training deep hedging strategies against adversarial distribution shifts improves their robustness and out-of-sample performance in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: A fluent summary can still contain claims that its source does not support. This paper asks whether automatic factuality metrics actually detect those inconsistencies or rely on superficial patterns. It examines both specialized evaluation models and methods that prompt a language model to judge factual consistency.

The authors use a shallow classifier to distinguish easy examples, where surface features suffice, from harder examples that require deeper reasoning. Every tested metric performs substantially worse on the harder group. Some metrics also respond more strongly to harmless edits than to corrections of factual errors. Building on that behavior, the authors show that most tested metrics can receive artificially higher scores when summaries gain innocuous sentences with no substantive content.

ChatGPT-DA, a prompting-based method, is the most robust and reliable among the tested metrics. However, the evidence suggests it may rely more on knowledge stored in the model than on the supplied source. The findings question whether high metric scores reliably indicate source-grounded factuality and motivate the paper’s recommendations for stronger benchmarks and evaluation methods.
neurips-2025-do-automatic-factuality-met.tldr: Factuality metrics struggle with reasoning-intensive examples, and most tested metrics can be fooled by adding content-free sentences.

paragraphs: This paper generates new views of moving scenes from a single-camera video by treating the task as an inverse problem. It uses a pretrained video diffusion model without changing its weights or adding auxiliary modules. The central intervention is to redesign the noise initialization from which the model generates video.

The authors identify an obstacle to deterministic inversion when the diffusion schedule ends with zero signal-to-noise ratio. They introduce K-order Recursive Noise Representation to address it and derive a closed-form expression. This representation enables efficient, precise alignment between the input’s VAE-encoded latent representation and the latents obtained through DDIM inversion, connecting the observed video to the diffusion process.

Changing the viewpoint also exposes regions that were hidden in the original video. Stochastic Latent Modulation handles this through visibility-aware sampling in latent space. Together, these components control how the input is represented and how unseen content is completed. The experiments demonstrate that structured manipulation at noise initialization can effectively produce dynamic novel views in this training-free setting.
neurips-2025-dynamic-view-synthesis-as-a.tldr: Structured noise initialization lets a pretrained video diffusion model synthesize new dynamic views without weight updates or auxiliary modules.

paragraphs: Rewarding only the final answer creates a problem for multimodal reasoning in multiple-choice tasks. A model can follow faulty reasoning and still guess the correct option, receiving the same reward as a sound solution. This paper introduces Self-Consistency Sampling to reduce the influence of those unreliable reasoning traces during reinforcement learning.

For each question, the method slightly perturbs the visual input and repeatedly truncates and resamples a reference reasoning trajectory. Agreement across the resulting trajectories produces a differentiable consistency score. That score downweights unreliable traces when updating the policy, adding a measure of stability to the information supplied by final-answer correctness.

The authors integrate the method into RLOO, GRPO, and the REINFORCE++ series. Across six multimodal benchmarks, they report accuracy improvements of up to 7.7 percentage points with negligible additional computation. The result supports consistency sampling as a practical addition to several outcome-reward training methods. Its role is to make lucky correct answers less influential by checking agreement across related trajectories, while retaining outcome rewards as part of training.
neurips-2025-enhancing-the-outcome-rewar.tldr: Self-Consistency Sampling downweights unreliable reasoning traces and improves multimodal outcome-reward training by up to 7.7 percentage points.

paragraphs: LogitGaze-Med predicts where a person looks and how long they look while searching medical images for diagnostic information. The paper argues that generic visual-language features and saliency signals can miss the detailed clinical meaning needed for this task. It therefore brings medical knowledge directly into a model of visual attention.

The framework combines domain-specific visual encoders, text embeddings of diagnostic labels, and semantic priors extracted through a logit-lens from LLaVA-Med. A multimodal transformer integrates these sources and directly predicts continuous fixation coordinates and dwell durations. These predictions form scanpaths: sequences describing the locations and timing of attention across an image.

Experiments use GazeSearch and expert-validated synthetic scanpaths generated from MIMIC-CXR. The authors report improvements of 20–30% in scanpath similarity metrics over competitive baselines. Incorporating predicted fixations as additional training data also produces gains above 5% in downstream pathology classification. The findings connect better modeling of clinically directed attention with improved classification in the reported experiments, showing a practical use for the predicted gaze information.
neurips-2025-from-human-attention-to-dia.tldr: LogitGaze-Med combines medical visual and language knowledge to predict scanpaths and improve downstream pathology classification.

paragraphs: ImgEdit addresses two obstacles to improving open-source image editing: limited high-quality training data and insufficient evaluation benchmarks. The dataset contains one million curated edit pairs, covering novel and complex single-turn edits as well as multi-turn tasks. This gives models examples of both individual changes and editing across a sequence of instructions.

The data construction pipeline combines a vision-language model, detection, segmentation, task-specific inpainting, and strict post-processing. The authors use the resulting data to train ImgEdit-E1, whose vision-language component processes both the reference image and the editing instruction. It outperforms existing open-source models on multiple tasks, supporting the value of the dataset together with the model design.

The accompanying ImgEdit-Bench evaluates instruction adherence, editing quality, and preservation of details. It includes basic tests, challenging single-turn cases, and a dedicated multi-turn suite. By evaluating proprietary models, open-source models, and ImgEdit-E1 within this structure, the paper connects training resources with a broader assessment of editing behavior. The benchmark separates following the requested change from producing a good-looking result and retaining image details.
neurips-2025-imgedit-a-unified-image-edi.tldr: ImgEdit supplies one million editing pairs, a trained editing model, and a benchmark covering instruction following, quality, and detail preservation.

paragraphs: LayerCraft aims to make image generation and repeated editing easier to control. It addresses spatial composition, consistency of objects, and changes made over multiple steps. The framework uses language models as coordinating agents to turn simple prompts into structured plans for generating and editing layered images.

A coordinator works with ChainArchitect, which uses stepwise reasoning to break a scene into components and plan object placement. The Object Integration Network then supports inserting and customizing objects with off-the-shelf text-to-image models, without retraining those models. Layered integration is designed to preserve an object’s identity while fitting it into the surrounding context and visual style.

The paper presents applications including batch collage editing and narrative scene generation. These illustrate how users can iteratively place, customize, and refine characters or props across images with limited manual effort. The contribution is a modular workflow that connects planning with image editing: spatial decisions become explicit, and object integration becomes a distinct part of the process. The abstract describes these capabilities and applications without reporting a numerical performance comparison.
neurips-2025-layercraft-enhancing-text-t.tldr: LayerCraft coordinates language-model planning and layered object integration to support controllable image generation and iterative editing without retraining.

paragraphs: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning adapts large models while limiting training resources, but its learning behavior is not fully understood. This paper studies adaptation through linearization, which approximates how a model changes around its pretrained parameters. It makes the tendency to stay near those parameters explicit by penalizing their Euclidean distance from the starting point.

Under this formulation, the authors connect fine-tuning dynamics to learning with a positive-definite neural tangent kernel. They analyze how closely the relevant optimization formulations agree as regularization strength changes. This matters because the usefulness of a linear explanation depends on whether it remains a good approximation in the fine-tuning regime being considered.

When linearization is appropriate, the paper finds a strong correlation between the kernel’s eigenvalue spectrum and adaptation performance. It also bounds how selecting different layers for fine-tuning changes that spectrum. Experiments with LoRA on language models validate the theory. These results offer a conditional explanation of adaptation and a possible basis for more informed parameter-efficient methods, rather than establishing that linearization describes every fine-tuning setting.
neurips-2025-linearization-explains-fine.tldr: A regularized linearization analysis connects fine-tuning performance to neural tangent kernel spectra when the linear approximation is appropriate.

paragraphs: Metis treats speech generation as a collection of tasks that can share a pretrained foundation. It first learns from large amounts of unlabeled speech, then adapts through task-specific fine-tuning. This separates learning general speech structure from learning how to respond to the inputs required by a particular application.

The model uses two discrete speech representations: tokens derived from self-supervised speech features and acoustic tokens obtained by quantizing waveforms. Pretraining uses masked generation on the self-supervised tokens across 300,000 hours of speech, without additional conditioning. Fine-tuning introduces task-specific conditions and supports multimodal inputs, including settings with limited adaptation data and trainable parameters.

The experiments cover zero-shot text-to-speech, voice conversion, target speaker extraction, speech enhancement, and lip-to-speech. Metis outperforms state-of-the-art task-specific or multitask systems across these five tasks, including configurations with fewer than 20 million trainable parameters or 300 times less training data. Those efficiency claims concern the reported adaptation settings alongside a large pretraining investment. The findings support sharing a speech foundation across substantially different generation tasks.
neurips-2025-metis-a-foundation-speech-g.tldr: Metis learns from unlabeled speech through masked pretraining and adapts efficiently to five speech generation tasks.

paragraphs: Neural MJD forecasts time series by explicitly representing both evolving random variation and abrupt jumps. The motivation is that non-stationary data can change its behavior over time, while sudden changes pose an additional challenge. The model formulates prediction as simulation of a stochastic differential equation learned with neural networks.

Its continuous component is a time-dependent Itô diffusion, while a time-dependent compound Poisson process represents jumps. To make learning tractable, the authors cap the number of jumps considered within short intervals when computing the likelihood. They provide a theoretical bound on the error introduced by this approximation, connecting computational simplification to a quantified approximation cost.

The paper also introduces an Euler–Maruyama solver with restart. Relative to the standard solver, it has a provably lower error bound for estimating expected states and reduced variance. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets report consistent improvements over state-of-the-art deep learning and statistical methods. The contribution combines an explicit model of changing stochastic behavior with learning and simulation procedures designed to make that model usable for forecasting.
neurips-2025-neural-mjd-neural-non-stati.tldr: Neural MJD combines time-varying diffusion and jump processes with tractable learning and an improved solver for time-series forecasting.

paragraphs: Diffusion classifiers identify an image’s category by comparing how a generative model denoises it under different category conditions. Their predictions can change substantially with the randomly sampled noise. Existing approaches stabilize classification by combining hundreds of noise samples, which makes classification slow. This paper investigates whether choosing noise more deliberately can address that instability.

The authors propose two principles for useful noise: it should disrupt particular frequency signals and particular spatial regions. Their NoOp method first optimizes a dataset-specific noise pattern for a given diffusion timestep. It then trains a meta-network that takes an image and predicts an image-specific noise offset. Adding these components produces the noise used in place of a random sample.

Ablation experiments across multiple datasets support the effectiveness of this optimization. The method changes the noise supplied to the classifier, making that input a learned part of classification rather than an uncontrolled source of variation. The authors also report that noise optimization is complementary to approaches such as prompt tuning and can benefit from combining with them.
neurips-2025-noise-matters-optimizing-ma.tldr: NoOp learns dataset-level noise and image-specific adjustments to address instability in diffusion-based image classification.

paragraphs: Neural combinatorial optimization models can construct strong solutions, but their internal representations offer little immediate explanation of their decisions. This paper investigates what information those representations contain through a collection of probing tasks. The goal is to make the learned knowledge more accessible to researchers and users studying these models.

The authors introduce Coefficient Significance Probing, which examines both probe coefficients and their statistical significance. Their experiments find that models encode low-level information needed to construct solutions alongside higher-level knowledge useful for decisions. The probing method also identifies particular embedding dimensions associated with specific knowledge and reveals differences in the biases that models impose on their representations.

The analysis uncovers evidence related to generalization, and the authors use the resulting insights to improve the analyzed model’s generalization through minor code changes. This provides a concrete example of interpretation informing model development. The broader contribution is a systematic approach to inspecting internal representations, with results that make probing a promising tool for understanding neural optimization models and identifying potentially useful changes.
neurips-2025-probing-neural-combinatoria.tldr: Coefficient Significance Probing reveals knowledge encoded in neural optimization models and helps inform a demonstrated generalization improvement.

paragraphs: Weather forecast quality is difficult to communicate with a numerical score alone. Traditional metrics capture some errors but offer less descriptive detail and understanding of changing weather patterns than expert assessment. RadarQA explores using a multimodal language model to connect key physical attributes of radar forecasts with detailed evaluation reports.

The paper defines tasks for both individual frames and sequences, with settings that require ratings or written assessments. To support these tasks, the authors build RQA-70K using an annotation pipeline that combines meteorological expert labels with automated heuristics. The dataset includes varying difficulty levels, providing material for both training and benchmarking.

RadarQA uses a multistage training strategy that progressively improves performance. In the reported experiments, it outperforms existing general multimodal language models across all evaluation settings. The findings support specialized training and data for forecast analysis, including analysis of how patterns evolve over time. The contribution centers on evaluating and describing forecast quality, with a task framework and dataset that make these capabilities measurable.
neurips-2025-radarqa-multi-modal-quality.tldr: RadarQA combines specialized training and expert-informed data to rate and describe weather radar forecast quality.

paragraphs: This paper finds that substantial gains from reinforcement-learning fine-tuning can accompany changes to only 5–30% of a language model’s parameters. The remaining parameters stay effectively unchanged. The phenomenon appears across all seven training algorithms and ten models examined, even though training includes no explicit requirement for sparse updates.

Fine-tuning just the identified subnetwork recovers test accuracy and produces a model nearly identical to full fine-tuning. Subnetworks also overlap across random seeds, datasets, and algorithms more than chance would predict. The sparsity is distributed through nearly all parameter matrices, rather than being concentrated in a few layers. At the same time, most update matrices are nearly full-rank, showing that changing relatively few entries can still span nearly all the represented dimensions.

The authors conjecture that this behavior primarily arises from training on data close to the policy’s own distribution. They find limited influence from KL regularization and gradient clipping. The empirical findings establish a recurring pattern in the tested systems, while the proposed explanation for its cause remains a conjecture.
neurips-2025-reinforcement-learning-fine.tldr: Across the tested models and algorithms, reinforcement-learning fine-tuning mainly changes a small, recurring subset of parameters distributed throughout the model.

paragraphs: Second-order optimization uses curvature information as well as gradients to guide learning. Although this can accelerate convergence under well-behaved noise, unusually large random deviations can make such methods unstable. This paper develops a theoretical account of second-order optimization when the noise has heavy tails.

The analysis assumes that stochastic gradients and Hessians have bounded p-th moments for some p greater than one and at most two. Under that condition, the authors establish tight lower bounds on how many samples any second-order method needs. They then construct a normalized stochastic gradient method that uses second-order information and matches those bounds, connecting a fundamental limit with an achievable algorithm.

A further algorithm clips both gradients and Hessians to control large deviations. Its high-probability upper bounds nearly match the fundamental limits. These results distinguish exact matching by the normalized method from near-matching guarantees for the clipping-based method. Together, they characterize sample requirements in the studied heavy-tailed setting and give Hessian clipping a theoretical basis as a robustness strategy.
neurips-2025-second-order-optimization-u.tldr: The paper establishes sample-complexity limits under heavy-tailed noise and develops second-order methods with matching or nearly matching guarantees.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning can weaken a language model’s safety alignment even when only a few training examples are harmful. A common defense assigns a safety weight to each complete example. This paper argues that such treatment is too coarse because a response can shift between harmless and harmful content as it unfolds.

Dynamic safety shaping instead adjusts learning within the response. The authors repurpose guardrail models to assess partial responses, tracking changes in risk segment by segment. This produces Safety Trajectory Assessment of Response, or STAR, a token-level signal that can guide how strongly different parts of the training sequence affect the model.

The resulting STAR-guided method reinforces learning from safe segments while suppressing unsafe content. Across the reported threats, datasets, and model families, it substantially improves safety without compromising capability on the intended tasks. The findings support using the evolving safety context of a response during fine-tuning. The central contribution is the finer control made possible by turning guardrail assessments into a signal that changes throughout a training example.
neurips-2025-shape-it-up-restoring-llm-s.tldr: STAR-guided dynamic safety shaping adjusts learning within responses to improve fine-tuning safety while preserving tested task capabilities.

paragraphs: Federated learning must manage both communication costs and privacy. Sketching compresses the model updates clients transmit, while the Gaussian mechanism clips updates and adds noise to provide client-level differential privacy. This paper studies their combined privacy behavior instead of analyzing the two mechanisms separately.

The Sketched Gaussian Mechanism receives a joint analysis using Rényi differential privacy. The resulting guarantee is sharper and more flexible than an isolated analysis. For fixed noise magnitude, the paper proves that its privacy level scales proportionally to one over the square root of the sketching dimension. For moderate sketch dimensions, the authors show that this can yield substantially stronger privacy guarantees than the original Gaussian mechanism under the same noise budget.

The mechanism supports both gradient descent and adaptive server optimizers. The convergence results depend only logarithmically on the number of model parameters. At equal privacy levels, experiments find sketched private learning competitive with non-sketching variants and better in some settings. Adaptive server optimization further improves empirical performance while preserving the privacy guarantees.
neurips-2025-sketched-gaussian-mechanism.tldr: Jointly analyzing sketching and Gaussian noise yields sharper privacy guarantees and competitive private federated learning performance.

paragraphs: Process reward models score intermediate reasoning steps, but using those scores for reinforcement fine-tuning can encourage reward hacking. This paper identifies summing discounted future rewards as the primary cause in its analysis: a model can exploit highly rewarded steps without producing reliably sound reasoning. PURE changes how these step-level rewards determine training credit.

Its value function uses the minimum future reward, making the weakest future score central to evaluation. The authors argue that this aligns training with how process rewards are used at test time, limits value ranges, and assigns advantages more rationally. Across three base models, this approach achieves reasoning performance similar to training with verifiable rewards, whereas conventional summation causes early training collapse.

Adding one-tenth verifiable rewards further reduces reward hacking. The best reported Qwen2.5-Math-7B-based model reaches 82.5% accuracy on AMC23 and 53.3% average accuracy across five benchmarks. The paper also analyzes encountered hacking cases and collapse. Its findings show that the way step rewards are combined can strongly affect whether process supervision supports useful training.
neurips-2025-stop-summation-min-form-cre.tldr: PURE uses minimum future process rewards for credit assignment, substantially reducing reward hacking in the reported reasoning experiments.

paragraphs: Four-dimensional Gaussian splatting represents moving scenes while retaining fast rendering, but its many Gaussian elements and repeated temporal information require substantial storage. This paper develops an end-to-end compression framework that explicitly balances representation size against rendering distortion. It builds on Ex4DGS while adapting ideas from compression of static Gaussian scenes.

The key temporal component uses a wavelet transform to exploit the prior that real-world motion is smooth. Instead of storing each point’s trajectory independently, the representation uses this structure to improve storage efficiency. The framework also accounts for entropy in compression, making storage cost part of the optimization rather than an afterthought.

Users can control the tradeoff between compression and rendering quality. In the reported experiments, compression reaches up to 91 times relative to the original Ex4DGS model while retaining high visual fidelity. This result supports the framework’s potential for storing, transmitting, and rendering dynamic scenes across different computational environments. The maximum compression figure is an observed result, while the adjustable tradeoff is the mechanism for accommodating different quality and resource requirements.
neurips-2025-temporal-smoothness-aware-r.tldr: A rate-distortion framework exploits smooth motion to compress Ex4DGS scenes by up to 91 times while maintaining high visual fidelity.

paragraphs: Natural scenes and movies create complex patterns of activity in the visual brain. Those patterns change over time, so a useful compact representation needs to account for temporal relationships. This paper introduces TE-ViDS, a sequential latent-variable model designed to extract such representations from visual neural activity.

TE-ViDS maps neural recordings into low-dimensional latent states that evolve over time. It divides those states into two parts and uses contrastive learning to shape their representations. These design choices aim to align the model with the characteristics of visual neural responses and retain information relevant to the stimulus.

Experiments on synthetic data and recordings from mouse visual cortex report the best decoding performance among the evaluated approaches for naturalistic scenes and movies. The learned trajectories are also interpretable and reveal underlying neural dynamics. Analyses provide insights into differences between subjects and cortical regions. Together, the findings suggest that explicitly modeling temporal structure can produce representations useful both for decoding visual information and for examining how visual processing differs across the recorded biological systems.
neurips-2025-time-evolving-dynamical-sys.tldr: TE-ViDS learns evolving compact representations of mouse visual activity that improve stimulus decoding and reveal interpretable neural dynamics.

paragraphs: Vision-language models can spend substantial computation processing image tokens that are redundant for a particular task. This becomes especially costly with high-resolution images and long videos. VCM introduces vision concept modeling, in which the model extracts relevant visual concepts according to the instruction it receives.

The framework learns from correlations between vision and language across different instances, without requiring expensive annotations of individual concepts. A forward-backward optimization algorithm lets the model adjust both the granularity of its concepts and their spatial alignment. The intended effect is an adaptive representation whose detail and organization reflect the task being requested.

Experiments report substantial computational savings while maintaining strong performance across several vision-language tasks. For LLaVA-1.5-7B, the reduction reaches up to 85% fewer floating-point operations. The findings support instruction-dependent concept extraction as a way to reduce visual processing costs. The contribution combines compression with learned semantic organization, so the model can vary which visual information it emphasizes instead of processing every input with the same token-level workload.
neurips-2025-vcm-vision-concept-modeling.tldr: VCM learns instruction-relevant visual concepts, reducing computation by up to 85% for LLaVA-1.5-7B while maintaining strong task performance.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a moving scene from a single-camera video is ambiguous because changes in appearance can reflect both structure and motion. ViDAR addresses the scarcity of viewpoint supervision by using personalized video diffusion models to synthesize additional views. These generated views supervise a Gaussian splatting representation of the scene over time.

Conditioning on scene-specific features helps recover fine appearance details and reduce artifacts associated with monocular ambiguity. However, generated views can disagree across space and time. ViDAR addresses that issue with a diffusion-aware loss and camera-pose optimization that align the synthetic views with the underlying scene geometry.

On DyCheck, which includes extreme viewpoint variation, the framework outperforms all compared state-of-the-art baselines in visual quality and geometric consistency. The authors particularly emphasize improvements in dynamic regions and introduce a benchmark for comparing reconstruction of motion-rich scene areas. The findings support using generated multiview supervision together with mechanisms that account for its inconsistencies, connecting diffusion-based synthesis to reconstruction of both scene appearance and motion.
neurips-2025-vidar-video-diffusion-aware.tldr: ViDAR uses personalized diffusion-generated views and geometry-aware alignment to improve dynamic scene reconstruction from single-camera video.
